topics.summary: A flower, a butterfly, a rangoli and a pinwheel all repeat a part in a definite pattern, and a cloud does not.

content.text:
Look around you, you may find many objects that catch your attention. Some such things are shown below: [Flower, Butterfly, Rangoli, Pinwheel]
There is something beautiful about the pictures above.
The flower looks the same from many different angles. What about the butterfly? No doubt, the colours are very attractive. But what else about the butterfly appeals to you?
On the other hand, look at this picture of clouds. There is no such repetitive pattern.
We can say that the first four figures are symmetrical and the last one is not symmetrical. A symmetry refers to a part or parts of a figure that are repeated in some definite pattern.

2. Each one has a part that comes back again in a fixed pattern. A cloud has no such repeat.
3. When a part of a figure repeats in a definite pattern we say the figure is symmetrical.

media.title: Fold and Find Lines
media.context: Class 6 NCERT Ganita Prakash ch 9 'Symmetry' (Line Symmetry). Fold a shape on a line. Do both halves match? Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description:
A sheet of paper lies on the screen with one figure printed on it, and a long dashed fold line lies across the figure. The student can drag the fold line to any place and turn it to a vertical, horizontal or slanted direction. Beside the sheet are a Fold button, an overlap meter that reads from 0 to 100 percent, and a list headed Lines found.

The student first says Yes or No to the question: will this fold work? Then the student presses Fold. One side of the figure flips over the line while a faint ghost stays where the other side was. If the halves overlap exactly, the meter reads 100 percent, the line turns green and is added to the list. If a corner sticks out, the part that does not match is shown in red and the meter stays below 100, so a figure that only looks balanced is seen not to fold onto itself. On a rectangle that is not a square, the vertical and horizontal folds work, but the fold along a diagonal leaves two red corners. Pressing Fold again opens the sheet for the next try, and the student can try as many lines as needed.

The six figures are an isosceles triangle (1 line), a square (4 lines: vertical, horizontal and both diagonals), a rectangle that is not a square (2 lines, and the diagonal fails), a kite that is not a rhombus (1 line), a scalene triangle (no line) and a regular hexagon (6 lines). After trying folds, the student keeps the lines that overlap and enters how many there are, and 0 is allowed for none. A wrong count shows the lines found so far on the figure and asks the student to try another direction. A solved card shows every line of symmetry as a dashed line with the two halves overlapping.

Hints come in order. First: what does it mean for two halves to overlap exactly? Then: try a vertical, a horizontal and a slanted fold on the figure. Then: press Fold on a line and look for any part that sticks out. Last, the lines that overlap are shown as dashed lines, and a similar figure follows. Through doing, the student learns that a line is a line of symmetry only when folding along it makes the two parts overlap exactly, and that a figure can have one line, several lines or none.

topics.summary: A line that folds a figure into two parts that exactly overlap is a line of symmetry.

content.text:
Figure (a) shows the picture of a blue triangle with a dotted line. What if you fold the triangle along the dotted line? Yes, one half of the triangle covers the other half completely. These are called mirror halves!
What about Figure (b) with the four puzzle pieces and a dotted line passing through the middle? Are they mirror halves? No, when we fold along the line, the left half does not exactly fit over the right half.

content.text:
Worked example: A blue triangle has a dotted line down its middle. If you fold the triangle along the dotted line, does one half cover the other half completely? Now look at four puzzle pieces joined together with a dotted line through the middle. Are the two sides mirror halves?
1. Fold the triangle along the dotted line: the halves match exactly.
2. Fold the puzzle pieces along their dotted line: the bumps and holes on the two sides do not match.
3. Only an exact match gives mirror halves.
Answer: For the triangle: yes, one half covers the other exactly, so they are mirror halves. For the puzzle pieces: no, when folded along the line the left half does not exactly fit over the right half.

topics.summary: A figure can have several lines of symmetry; try every fold and count those whose halves overlap.

content.text:
Does a square have only one line of symmetry?
Take a square piece of paper. By folding, find all its lines of symmetry.
Here are the different folds giving different lines of symmetry.
Fold the paper into half vertically.
Fold it again into half horizontally (i.e., you have folded it twice). Now open out the folds.
Again fold the square into half (for a third time now), but this time along a diagonal, as shown in the figure. Again, open it.
Fold it into half (for the fourth time), but this time along the other diagonal, as shown in the figure. Open out the fold.
Is there any other way to fold the square so that the two halves overlap? How many lines of symmetry does the square shape have?

content.text:
1. Predict first: does a square have only one line of symmetry? How many folds do you think work?
2. Fold it in half vertically, then horizontally: two lines of symmetry.
3. Fold along one diagonal and then the other: two more lines, in all 4.
4. No other fold makes the two halves overlap, so the square has exactly 4 lines of symmetry.

source: Draw the following. (a) A triangle with exactly one line of symmetry. (b) A triangle with exactly three lines of symmetry. (c) A triangle with no line of symmetry. Is it possible to draw a triangle with exactly two lines of symmetry?
never_show: the verdict on exactly two lines before the answer beat
maths_rules: A line of symmetry is a fold line along which one half covers the other exactly.
A triangle with exactly two equal sides has exactly one line, from the corner where the equal sides meet to the middle of the third side.
A triangle with all three sides equal has three lines, one from each corner to the middle of the opposite side.
A triangle with all sides different has no line.
If a triangle had two lines, then two pairs of sides would be equal, which makes all three sides equal and gives three lines. So exactly two lines is not possible.
Check: count the folds again on each drawn triangle.

content.text:
$1$. Two equal sides give one line: the line from the apex to the middle of the base.
$2$. All three sides equal give three lines.
$3$. If a triangle has two lines of symmetry it is forced to have all three, so exactly two cannot happen.
Answer: $(a)$: An isosceles triangle (two equal sides, third side different). $(b)$: An equilateral triangle. $(c)$: A scalene triangle (all sides different). No, it is not possible to draw a triangle with exactly two lines of symmetry.

media.title: Mirror Completer
media.context: Class 6 NCERT Ganita Prakash ch 9 'Symmetry' (Line Symmetry). Complete the shape across the mirror line. Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description:
A square grid fills the screen. One bold blue mirror line runs across it, and half of a figure is drawn on one side, with its corners marked as dots. A Reflect button sits below the grid, and the later cards show a second blue line.

For each corner dot the student first predicts where its mirror partner will land, then taps or drags to that grid point. A dashed link at once joins the dot to the partner and crosses the blue line at right angles, with equal tick marks drawn on the two sides to show the distances to the line. If the partner is on the wrong side, or at a different distance, the link shows the unequal distances and the student moves the partner. A dot that already sits on the line cannot go anywhere: it is shown staying fixed, with its partner on top of itself. Pressing Reflect checks the partners placed, or drops the missing ones one by one if the student is stuck. When every partner is down, the student joins the dots in order to finish the figure.

The six cards are: a vertical line with a 3-square L-shape on one side; a horizontal line with a triangle touching it, whose corners on the line stay put; a diagonal line with a one-square staircase, where the dashed link slants and still meets the line at right angles; a vertical line that the figure crosses, so points on both sides are reflected; two lines, vertical and horizontal, with a small shape in one corner, where the student reflects in the first line and then reflects the whole figure in the second to get 4 copies in all; and two diagonal lines with a small shape in one gap, again 4 copies in all. A solved card shows the completed figure with its line, or lines, as dashed lines.

Hints come in order. First: which side of the line is the figure on now? Then: each point goes to the other side at the same distance from the line. Then: count the squares from the point to the line, and count the same number on the other side. Last, the partner is shown with its dashed link, and a similar figure follows. Through doing, the student learns that every point and its mirror partner are the same distance from the line on opposite sides, that points on the line stay where they are, and that two lines of symmetry are used one after the other.

topics.summary: Reflecting in a line of symmetry swaps each point with its mirror partner on the other side.

content.text:
So far we have been saying that when we fold a figure along a line of symmetry, the two parts overlap completely. We could also say that the part of the figure on one side of the line of symmetry is reflected by the line to the other side; similarly, the part of the figure on the other side of the line of symmetry is reflected to the first side! Let us understand this by labeling some points on the figure.
The figure shows a square with its corners labeled A, B, C and D. Let us first consider the vertical line of symmetry. When we reflect the square along this line, the points B, C on the right get reflected to the left side and occupy the positions occupied earlier by A, D. What happens to the points A, D? A occupies the position occupied by B and D that of C!

content.text:
Worked example: A square has corners labelled A (top left), B (top right), C (bottom right), D (bottom left). When the square is reflected along the vertical line of symmetry, where do A, B, C and D go?
1. Draw the vertical line through the middle.
2. Each corner moves to the matching corner on the other side of the line, at the same height.
Answer: B and C go to the positions earlier held by A and D, and A and D go to the positions earlier held by B and C: A takes the place of B, B the place of A, D the place of C and C the place of D.

media.title: Punch and Unfold
media.context: Class 6 NCERT Ganita Prakash ch 9 'Symmetry' (Line Symmetry). Fold, punch a hole, and predict the pattern. Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description:
A square sheet of paper lies flat in the middle of the screen. Beside it are three fold buttons, vertical, horizontal and diagonal, a fold counter with a layer count that starts at 1, a Punch tool, a Cut tool and an Unfold button.

The student chooses folds and the sheet folds with a short animation. Each fold halves the shape and doubles the layers, so after a vertical fold and then a horizontal fold the layer count reads 4. The student predicts how many holes the opened sheet will have, then taps the folded sheet with Punch, or draws one straight line across its edge with Cut, and presses Unfold. The sheet opens to show the holes, and every fold is drawn as a dashed line. The student can see that each hole has a mirror partner across each fold line, and that a fold line sits halfway between a pair of matching holes, at right angles to the line joining them.

The six cards are: one vertical fold and one punch, how many holes (2); a diagonal fold and one punch (2 holes); a vertical fold then a horizontal fold and one punch (4 holes); two holes on the left and right at the same height, which fold made them (vertical); four holes, one near each corner, from a single punch, which folds (vertical and horizontal); and a square hole in the centre using folds and one straight cut across the corner that meets the centre of the sheet. For the last card two different pairs of folds work. A vertical and a horizontal fold give a square tilted like a diamond, and two diagonal folds give a square with its sides parallel to the sheet, so the student makes both. A wrong fold shows where the punched holes would land and how they differ from the target, and a solved card shows the sheet folded, punched and opened in three small pictures.

Hints come in order. First: how many layers does the folded sheet have? Then: each layer gets one hole, so the holes are mirror partners across each fold. Then: the fold line sits halfway between a pair of matching holes. Last, the fold lines are shown dashed, and a similar card follows. Through doing, the student learns that every fold doubles the holes or cuts, and that the folds of a paper cut-out become the lines of symmetry of the opened shape.

topics.summary: A fold is a line of symmetry: anything marked or cut on a folded sheet appears twice or more, mirrored, when the sheet is opened.

content.text:
So far we have seen symmetrical figures and asymmetrical figures. How does one generate such symmetrical figures? Let us explore this.
Ink Blot Devils
You enjoyed doing this earlier in Class 5. Take a piece of paper. Fold it in half. Open the paper and spill a few drops of ink (or paint) on one half.
Now press the halves together and then open the paper again.
What do you see?
Is the resulting figure symmetric?
If yes, where is the line of symmetry?
Is there any other line along which it can be folded to produce two identical parts?
Try making more such patterns.

2. Each fold doubles the copies: one fold gives 2, two folds give 4, three folds give 8.
3. Every fold line becomes a line of symmetry of the opened design.

content.text:
Worked example: Make different symmetric shapes by folding and cutting. Use thin rectangular coloured paper, fold it several times and cut out intricate patterns, like the blue star-shaped cut-outs shown. Identify the lines of symmetry in the repeating design.
1. Fold the paper several times.
2. Cut some shapes along the edges and corners.
3. Open it: every crease is a line of symmetry of the repeating design.
Answer: Any such cut-out is symmetric about each of its fold lines. For example, the eight-pointed star shown has 8 lines of symmetry.

maths_rules: A hole and its partner are mirror pictures, so the fold line is the line of symmetry between them
The fold line is halfway between the two holes and at a right angle to the line joining them
Two holes left and right at the same height: the line joining them is horizontal, so the fold is vertical, through the middle
Two holes close together near the top right corner: the fold is the diagonal from bottom left to top right, between the two holes
Two holes on the right edge, one above the other: the line joining them is vertical, so the fold is horizontal, through the middle
One fold gives 2 layers and 2 holes; 2 folds give 2 x 2 = 4 layers and 4 holes
Four holes from a single punch: fold vertically, then horizontally (or the other way round); the one hole goes through 4 layers
Check: folding the opened sheet along the line puts each hole on its partner

$1$. The fold line is the line of symmetry, halfway between each pair of matching holes and at right angles to the line joining them.
$2$. For $(d)$, four holes means two lines of symmetry: fold in half, then in half again.
Answer: $(a)$: a vertical fold through the middle; $(b)$: a diagonal fold (from bottom left to top right) between the two holes; $(c)$: a horizontal fold through the middle between the two holes; $(d)$: the paper was folded vertically and then horizontally (or the other way round), and one hole was punched through all four layers.

media.title: Turn and Match
media.context: Class 6 NCERT Ganita Prakash ch 9 'Symmetry' (Rotational Symmetry). Turn a shape. When does it match itself? Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description:
The student sees a figure drawn in colour on top of a faint fixed outline of itself, with a red dot marking the centre of rotation. Below it is a turn dial from 0 to 360 degrees in steps of 15 degrees, a Turn button and a record of the angles that matched.

The student first predicts the smallest turn that will make the figure look the same. Then the student sets the dial, presses Turn, and the figure rotates about the red dot. If the figure fits exactly on its outline, the outline flashes green and the angle can be added to the record. A turn that nearly fits shows the gap in red, so a near miss cannot be recorded. The student keeps turning, noting each angle that matches, and finally lists the angles in order with 360 last. A list that leaves out 360 is reminded that a full turn always matches.

The six figures are a 4-bladed windmill (90, 180, 270 and 360 degrees), a strip with one short side (360 degrees only, because at 180 degrees the short side lands on the wrong end), a plus shape with 4 equal arms (90, 180, 270 and 360), a long rectangle that is not a square (180 and 360), a figure with 3 equal arms 120 degrees apart (120, 240 and 360), and an isosceles triangle that is not equilateral (360 only). The windmill's solved card points out that no fold makes it overlap, yet it matches by turning. A solved card shows the matching positions in colour around the centre.

Hints come in order. First: where is the centre of rotation marked? Then: turn the figure slowly and watch for the outline to match. Then: note each angle where it matches, and add 360 at the end. Last, the matching angles are shown in colour, and a similar figure follows. Through doing, the student learns that a figure has rotational symmetry when some turn below 360 degrees matches it, that 360 degrees always matches, and that a figure whose only match is 360 degrees has no rotational symmetry.

maths_rules: A turn about the centre after which a shape looks exactly the same is called an angle of symmetry
A shape that matches itself after a turn smaller than the full turn has rotational symmetry
A half turn of 180 degrees puts the longer side of the strip on top, where the start picture has the shorter side, so the strip does not overlap itself
A quarter turn and a three quarter turn stand the flat sides upright, but the strip has no upright sides, so they do not fit either
Two half turns make 360 degrees, which brings the strip back, so only the full turn works
The strip has no rotational symmetry

topics.summary: A figure has rotational symmetry when a turn between 0° and 360° about its centre makes it look the same; 360° always works.

content.text:
The paper windmill in the picture looks symmetrical but there is no line of symmetry! However, if you fold it, the two halves will not exactly overlap. On the other hand, if you rotate it by 90° about the red point at the centre, the windmill looks exactly the same.
We say that the windmill has rotational symmetry.
When talking of rotational symmetry, there is always a fixed point about which the object is rotated. This fixed point is called the centre of rotation.
Will the windmill above look exactly the same when rotated through an angle of less than 90°?
No!
An angle through which a figure can be rotated to look exactly the same is called an angle of rotational symmetry, or just an angle of symmetry, for short.
For the windmill, the angles of symmetry are 90° (quarter turn), 180° (half turn), 270° (three-quarter turn) and 360° (full turn). Observe that when any figure is rotated by 360°, it comes back to its original position, so 360° is always an angle of symmetry.
Thus, we see that the windmill has 4 angles of symmetry.
Do you know of any other shape that has exactly four angles of symmetry?

2. The blades do not land on the blades again.
3. The first turn that makes it look the same is 90°, so no smaller angle works.

content.text:
Worked example: The windmill has exactly 4 angles of symmetry: 90°, 180°, 270° and 360°. Do you know of any other shape that has exactly four angles of symmetry?
1. A shape with 4 angles of symmetry matches itself after each quarter turn.
2. A square does this: 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°.
3. A plus sign with 4 equal arms does the same.
Answer: Yes, a square (also a plus sign made of 4 equal arms, or a pinwheel with 4 equal blades).

content.text:
Worked example: How many angles of symmetry does a square have? How much rotation does it require to get the initial square?
1. Rotate the square about its centre by a quarter turn: it overlaps itself.
2. Each further quarter turn does the same: 90°, 180°, 270°.
3. A full turn of 360° brings every corner back to its own place.
Answer: 4 angles of symmetry: 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°. The square overlaps itself after a 90° rotation (A goes to B, B to C, C to D, D to A); it is back in its starting position after 360°.

content.text:
Worked example: A square gets back onto itself after a 90° rotation. Do you know where to mark the centre of rotation?
1. The centre of rotation is the fixed point that does not move.
2. In a square this is the middle point.
3. It is where the diagonals meet.
Answer: At the centre of the square, the point where its two diagonals cross.

2. Rotate by 270° (three-quarter turn): it overlaps itself.
3. Rotate by 360° (full turn): it is back where it started.
Answer: 180°, 270° and 360°.

Example: Find the angles of symmetry of the following strip.
Solution: Let us rotate the strip in a clockwise direction about its centre.
A rotation of 180° results in the figure above. Does this overlap with the original figure.
No. Why?
Another rotation through 180° from this position gives the original shape.
This figure comes back to its original shape only after one complete rotation through 360°. So, we say that this figure does not have rotational symmetry.

topics.detailed_summary: A figure has rotational symmetry when a turn between 0° and 360° about its centre makes it look the same; 360° always works.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students explain that a windmill with 4 equal blades looks the same after a 90° turn about its centre, and define the centre of rotation and an angle of symmetry.
Students list the angles of symmetry of a square and mark its centre of rotation at the crossing of the diagonals.
Students show by turning that a strip with one short side does not match itself after 180°, so its only angle of symmetry is 360°.
Students turn a figure about its marked centre on the tool, note each turn at which it matches itself, and list the angles of symmetry.

content.text:
$1$. Rotate the strip by $180^\circ$ about its centre: the longer side is now on top.
$2$. This does not overlap the original, because the top and bottom sides are different.
$3$. Another $180^\circ$ gives the original, so only the full turn $360^\circ$ works.
Answer: Only $360^\circ$. The strip does not have rotational symmetry.

five pointed star with its centre dot: a turn of 360 / 5 = 72 degrees fits
downward triangle with a dot, as drawn, and the B shape (a vertical line with two half circles on its right): fit only after 360 degrees

media.title: Radial Arms Builder
media.context: Class 6 NCERT Ganita Prakash ch 9 'Symmetry' (Rotational Symmetry). Space the arms evenly so the shape turns onto itself. Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description:
At the middle of the screen is a small centre point with identical arms reaching out from it, up to 8 of them. The student has a number-of-arms stepper, a slider for each angle between neighbouring arms, a Turn button and a list of angles of symmetry. A faint copy of the figure sits exactly over the fixed figure and is the part that turns.

The student predicts the angle of symmetry, sets the number of arms and the angles between them, then presses Turn. The copy rotates over the fixed figure and every turn at which the arms land exactly on arms is added to the list, with 360 last. The gaps always add up to a full turn of 360 degrees, so changing one gap changes the last one. If the angles are unequal, the copy fails to land on the figure and the gap is shown in red. The student can nudge one gap of an equal figure and watch the list shrink to just 360. The number of angles in the list, counting 360, is shown as the order of the figure.

The six figures are: 4 arms at 90 degrees (90, 180, 270 and 360); 4 arms where opposite arms point in opposite directions but the two pairs are not at right angles, for example gaps of 60, 120, 60 and 120 degrees (180 and 360 only); 3 arms at 120 degrees (120, 240 and 360); 3 arms with gaps of 100, 120 and 140 degrees (360 only); 5 arms at 72 degrees (72, 144, 216, 288 and 360); and 6 arms at 60 degrees (order 6). A wrong order shows the angles counted one by one along a clock face, and a solved card shows the angle between arms written as 360 divided by the number of arms.

Hints come in order. First: how many arms does the figure have, and are they all the same? Then: for equal arms, share the full turn of 360 degrees equally among the gaps. Then: divide 360 by the number of arms to get the gap and the smallest angle. Last, the angles are shown on a clock face, and a similar figure follows. Through doing, the student learns that equal arms at equal gaps of 360 divided by n give n angles of symmetry, that the order is the number of angles counting 360, and that unequal spacing can leave only 360.

content.text:
Consider this figure, a picture with 4 radial arms. How many angles of symmetry does it have? What are they? Note that the angle between adjacent central dotted lines is 90°.
Can you change the angles between the radial arms so that the figure still has 4 angles of symmetry? Try drawing it.
To check if the figure drawn indeed has 4 angles of symmetry, you could draw the figure on two different pieces of paper. Cut out the radial arms from one of the papers. Keep the figure on the paper fixed and rotate the cutout to check for rotational symmetry.

content.text:
Worked example: A picture has 4 radial arms (a plus-shaped figure with 4 equal arms), and the angle between adjacent central dotted lines is 90°. How many angles of symmetry does it have? What are they?
1. The arms are equal and 90° apart.
2. Each quarter turn moves an arm onto the next arm.
3. So the turns 90°, 180°, 270° and 360° all work.
Answer: 4 angles of symmetry: 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°.

content.text:
Worked example: Can you change the angles between the radial arms so that the figure still has 4 angles of symmetry? Try drawing it.
1. For 4 angles of symmetry, a quarter turn must put each arm on the next arm.
2. So all four angles between neighbouring arms must be equal.
3. They must add to 360°, so each is 90°.
Answer: Not if the arms are identical and only the angles are changed: the 4 arms must stay equally spaced, with 90° between neighbours. Changing the angles gives fewer angles of symmetry.

content.text:
Worked example: To check if a figure with radial arms has 4 angles of symmetry, draw it on two pieces of paper. Cut out the radial arms from one paper, keep the figure on the other paper fixed, and rotate the cutout to check for rotational symmetry.
1. Draw the figure twice and cut out one copy.
2. Pin the cutout at the centre and turn it over the other copy.
3. Count the turns after which it fits exactly.
Answer: A correct check shows the cutout fits exactly onto the fixed figure at 90°, 180°, 270° and 360° only.

content.text:
How will you modify the figure above so that it has only two angles of symmetry?
Here is one way:
We have seen figures having 4 and 2 angles of symmetry. Can we get a figure having exactly 3 angles of symmetry? Can you use radial arms for this?
Let us try with 3 radial arms as in the figure below. How many angles of symmetry does it have and what are they?
Here is a figure with three radial arms.
Trace and cut out a copy of this figure. By rotating the cutout over this figure determine its angles of rotation.
We see that only a full turn or a rotation of 360° will bring the figure back into itself. So this figure does not have rotational symmetry as 360 degrees is its only angle of symmetry.

Worked example: How will you modify the plus-shaped figure with 4 radial arms so that it has only two angles of symmetry?
1. Change the figure so a quarter turn no longer fits.
2. Keep it the same after a half turn (180°).
3. Then the angles of symmetry are only 180° and 360°.
Answer: Make opposite arms alike but the two pairs different, for example the book's figure where the top arm bends to the right at its end and the bottom arm bends to the left (a half turn copy), with the left and right arms straight. Then only 180° and 360° work.

content.text:
Worked example: Can we get a figure having exactly 3 angles of symmetry? Can you use radial arms for this?
1. 3 angles of symmetry means 3 turns that fit, including 360°.
2. 3 equal arms at equal gaps share the full turn equally.
3. Each gap is 360 ÷ 3 = 120°.
Answer: Yes: use 3 equal radial arms placed 120° apart.

content.text:
However, can anything in the figure be changed to make it have 3 angles of symmetry?
Can it be done by changing the angles between the dotted lines?
If a figure with three radial arms should have rotational symmetry, then a rotated version of it should overlap with the original. Here are rough diagrams of both of them.
If these two figures must overlap, what can you tell about the angles?
Observe that ∠A must overlap ∠B, ∠B must overlap ∠C and ∠C must overlap ∠A.
So, ∠A = ∠B = ∠C. What must this angle be?
We know that a full turn has 360 degrees. This is equally distributed amongst these three angles. So each angle must be 360°/3 = 120°.
So, the radial arms figure with 3 arms shows rotational symmetry when the angle between adjacent dotted lines is 120°. Use paper cutouts to verify this observation.
Now how many angles of rotation does the figure have and what are they?
Note: The colours have been added to show the rotations.

If a figure with three radial arms should have rotational symmetry, then a rotated version of it should overlap with the original. Here are rough diagrams of both of them.
If these two figures must overlap, what can you tell about the angles?
Observe that ∠A must overlap ∠B, ∠B must overlap ∠C and ∠C must overlap ∠A.
So, ∠A = ∠B = ∠C. What must this angle be?
We know that a full turn has 360 degrees. This is equally distributed amongst these three angles. So each angle must be 360°/3 = 120°.
So, the radial arms figure with 3 arms shows rotational symmetry when the angle between adjacent dotted lines is 120°. Use paper cutouts to verify this observation.
Now how many angles of rotation does the figure have and what are they?

4. The figure then turns onto itself at 120°, 240° and 360°.

Worked example: Can anything in the three-arm figure be changed to make it have 3 angles of symmetry? Can it be done by changing the angles between the dotted lines?

2. They share a full turn of 360°.
3. Each is 120°.
Answer: Yes, make all three angles between adjacent dotted lines equal to 120°.

1. ∠A must overlap ∠B, ∠B must overlap ∠C and ∠C must overlap ∠A.
2. So the three angles are equal.
3. They share 360°, so each is 360 ÷ 3 = 120°.
Answer: ∠A = ∠B = ∠C = 360 ÷ 3 = 120°.

Answer: ∠A = ∠B = ∠C = 360 ÷ 3 = 120°.

content.text:
Worked example: A 3-arm figure has 120° between adjacent arms. How many angles of rotation does it have and what are they?
1. After 120° each arm lands on the next arm.
2. After 240° (120° + 120°) it fits again.
3. After 360° (120° + 120° + 120°) it is back to the start.
Answer: 3 angles of symmetry: 120°, 240°, 360°.

media.title: Angle Ladder
media.context: Class 6 NCERT Ganita Prakash ch 9 'Symmetry' (Rotational Symmetry). Climb the ladder by turning. Where does it fit? Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description:
A round disc divided into 12 equal sectors sits on the left like a clock face, and a tall ladder marked from 0 to 360 degrees stands on the right. The student has a repeat-every stepper, a dial that tests a target angle and a read-out for the smallest angle.

In the first two cards the student colours the disc so that it has a given number of angles of symmetry. The student chooses how often the colour pattern repeats around the circle, colours that block of sectors, and the tool copies it all the way round. If the repeat divides 12, the copies close up and the disc matches itself after one repeat. If it does not, for example every 5 sectors, the pattern fails to close up and the leftover sectors show in red. A pattern that repeats every 4 sectors gives 3 angles of symmetry, and one that repeats every 3 sectors gives 4. Trying other repeats shows that only 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12 sectors close up.

In the other cards the ladder takes over. The student predicts the smallest angle before moving the stepper for the number of equal turns, and the rungs climb by that angle up to 360. With a smallest angle of 60 the other angles are 120, 180, 240, 300 and 360. When 60 is an angle and two angles lie below it, the student tests smaller angles on the dial and finds the smallest is 20, with rungs 20, 40 and 60. A smallest angle of 45 reaches 360 after 8 turns, so it is possible. For 17 the rungs reach 357 and then jump past 360, leaving a remainder of 3, and the read-out gives 360 divided by 17 as 21 and 3/17, which is not a whole number of turns, so 17 is not possible. Setting 7 equal turns gives 51 and 3/7 degrees in the same read-out.

Hints come in order. First: how many equal turns make one full turn? Then: the smallest angle is 360 divided by the number of turns. Then: every other angle is that angle added again and again, up to 360. Last, the ladder is shown rung by rung, and a similar card follows. Through doing, the student learns that the angles of symmetry are the multiples of the smallest angle, that 360 is always the top rung, and that a whole-number smallest angle must be a factor of 360.

content.text:
1. Predict first: for 5 equal arms, what is the angle between neighbours?
2. 360 ÷ 5 = 72°, so the angles of symmetry are 72°, 144°, 216°, 288° and 360°.
3. For 6 arms, 360 ÷ 6 = 60°.
4. For 7 arms, 360 ÷ 7 is 51 with remainder 3, so the smallest angle is 51 3/7°, not a whole number.

2. See what is stuck to each side: the same blue shape made of triangles.
3. Going around the boundary, the shape repeats in the same turned position each time.

content.text:
Let us list down the angles of symmetry for all the cases above.
• Angles of symmetry when there are exactly 2 of them: 180°, 360°.
• Angles of symmetry when there are exactly 3 of them: 120°, 240°, 360°.
• Angles of symmetry when there are exactly 4 of them: 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°.
Do you observe something common about the angles of symmetries in these cases? The first set of numbers are all multiples of 180. The second are all multiples of 120. The third are all multiples of 90.
In each case, the angles are the multiples of the smallest angle. You may wonder and ask if this will always happen. What do you think?
True or False
• Every figure will have 360 degrees as an angle of symmetry.
• If the smallest angle of symmetry of a figure is a natural number in degrees, then it is a factor of 360.

content.text:
$1$. For $n$ equal arms the gap between neighbours is $360 \div n$.
$2$. $5$ arms: $360 \div 5 = 72^\circ$. Multiples of $72^\circ$ up to $360^\circ$.
$3$. $6$ arms: $360 \div 6 = 60^\circ$. Multiples of $60^\circ$ up to $360^\circ$.
Answer: $(a)$: Yes, $5$ equal arms $72^\circ$ apart: $72^\circ$, $144^\circ$, $216^\circ$, $288^\circ$, $360^\circ$. $(b)$: Yes, $6$ equal arms $60^\circ$ apart: $60^\circ$, $120^\circ$, $180^\circ$, $240^\circ$, $300^\circ$, $360^\circ$.
steps: For n equal arms the gap between neighbours is 360 ÷ n.
5 arms: 360 ÷ 5 = 72°. Multiples of 72° up to 360°.
6 arms: 360 ÷ 6 = 60°. Multiples of 60° up to 360°.

content.text:
$1$. $7$ equal arms share the full turn of $360^\circ$.
$2$. $360 \div 7$ gives $51$ with remainder $3$.
$3$. So the smallest angle is $51 \frac{3}{7}$ degrees, not a whole number.
Answer: $360 \div 7$ is $51 \frac{3}{7}$ degrees. It is not a whole number.

concepts.concept_name: Order and the Smallest Angle of Symmetry: Q3

content.text:
$1$. Look at $120^\circ$, $240^\circ$, $360^\circ$: they are $1 \times 120^\circ$, $2 \times 120^\circ$ and $3 \times 120^\circ$.
$2$. Turning by the smallest angle twice is the same as turning by twice that angle.
$3$. So every angle of symmetry is a multiple of the smallest one.
Answer: Yes, the angles of symmetry are always multiples of the smallest angle of symmetry.
steps: Turning by the smallest angle twice is the same as turning by twice that angle.
So every angle of symmetry is a multiple of the smallest one.

content.text:
$1$. A full turn of $360^\circ$ always brings any figure back to itself.
$2$. The smallest angle fits a whole number of times in $360^\circ$.
$3$. So a whole-number smallest angle is a factor of $360$.
Answer: Both are True.

The circle is divided into $12$ equal sectors. (i): $3$ angles of symmetry (ii): $4$ angles of symmetry (iii): Possible numbers of angles of symmetry

content.text:
$1$. Each sector is $360 \div 12 = 30^\circ$.
$2$. $3$ angles of symmetry need a pattern that repeats every $120^\circ$, that is every $4$ sectors; $4$ angles need a pattern repeating every $90^\circ$, every $3$ sectors.
$3$. The pattern can repeat every $1$, $2$, $3$, $4$, $6$ or $12$ sectors, giving $12$, $6$, $4$, $3$, $2$ or $1$ angles of symmetry.
Answer: (i): Colour every $4\text{th}$ sector (with $3$ coloured sectors, $120^\circ$ apart). (ii): Colour every $3\text{rd}$ sector (with $4$ coloured sectors, $90^\circ$ apart). (iii): The number of angles of symmetry can be $1$, $2$, $3$, $4$, $6$ or $12$, which is at most $12$.

content.text: In a figure, $60^\circ$ is the smallest angle of symmetry. What are the other angles of symmetry of this figure?

content.publication_text: In a figure, $60^\circ$ is the smallest angle of symmetry. What are the other angles of symmetry of this figure?

content.text:
$1$. Other angles of symmetry are multiples of the smallest angle.
$2$. $60 \times 2 = 120^\circ$, $60 \times 3 = 180^\circ$, $60 \times 4 = 240^\circ$, $60 \times 5 = 300^\circ$.
$3$. $60 \times 6 = 360^\circ$ (full turn).
Answer: $120^\circ$, $180^\circ$, $240^\circ$, $300^\circ$, $360^\circ$.

content.text: In a figure, $60^\circ$ is an angle of symmetry. The figure has two angles of symmetry less than $60^\circ$. What is its smallest angle of symmetry?
content.question: In a figure, 60° is an angle of symmetry. The figure has two angles of symmetry less than 60°. What is its smallest angle of symmetry?
content.question_tex: In a figure, $60^\circ$ is an angle of symmetry. The figure has two angles of symmetry less than $60^\circ$. What is its smallest angle of symmetry?

content.text:
$1$. Angles of symmetry are multiples of the smallest angle.
$2$. Two angles less than $60^\circ$ means the smallest angle $d$ and $2d$ are below $60^\circ$, and $3d = 60^\circ$.
$3$. So $d = 60 \div 3 = 20^\circ$.
Answer: $20^\circ$

content.text:
$1$. The smallest angle must fit a whole number of times into $360^\circ$.
$2$. $(a)$: $360 \div 45 = 8$, so yes: $8$ equal arms.
$3$. $(b)$: $360 \div 17$ is not a whole number (since $17$ is not a factor of $360$), so no.
Answer: $(a)$: Yes. $(b)$: No.

content.text:
Is there a smallest angle of symmetry for all figures? It turns out that this is the case for most figures, except for the most symmetric shapes like the circle, whose symmetries we now discuss.
The circle is a fascinating figure. What happens when you rotate a circle clockwise about its centre? It coincides with itself. It does not matter what angle you rotate it by! So, for a circle, every angle is an angle of symmetry.

content.text:
Worked example: Is there a smallest angle of symmetry for all figures?
1. A figure like a square has smallest angle 90°.
2. A circle fits itself after any turn.
3. So there is no smallest angle for a circle.
Answer: No. Most figures have one, but a circle does not: every angle is an angle of symmetry for a circle.

media.title: Lines and Turns Sorter
media.context: Class 6 NCERT Ganita Prakash ch 9 'Symmetry' (Both Together, Tiles and a Game). Test each shape, then sort it by its symmetry. Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description:
A tray at the bottom holds the figures, and beside it is a two-way table with rows named has a line and has no line, and columns named has a turn and has no turn. Each figure has two buttons, a Fold test and a Turn test, and two counters, one for lines of symmetry and one for angles of symmetry. Here a turn means some angle below 360 degrees that matches.

The student picks a figure and predicts the box it belongs in. The Fold test lets the student set fold lines and press Fold, and every line that overlaps is drawn dashed on the figure and counted. The Turn test shows a red centre dot and a dial, and every angle that matches is marked and counted. The two tests are separate, and the student runs both before deciding. The student then drops the figure into a box and types its two counts. A figure dropped in the wrong box has both test results replayed beside it. A count of angles that ignores 360 is reminded that a full turn is always an angle of symmetry.

The six figures are an equilateral triangle (3 lines, 3 angles: 120, 240 and 360), a square (4 lines, 4 angles), a kite that is not a rhombus (1 line, and only 360, so 1 angle), a twisted six-petal flower (0 lines, 6 angles at steps of 60), a regular hexagon (6 lines, 6 angles) and a scalene triangle (0 lines, only 360). A solved card shows the fold lines and the matching turns on the figure.

Hints come in order. First: which test finds lines, and which finds turns? Then: run the fold test first, then turn the figure about its centre. Then: count the matching folds and the matching turns, including 360. Last, both results are shown on the figure, the box is filled and a similar figure follows. Through doing, the student learns that lines and turns are two separate tests whose answers can differ, that a figure can have lines only, turns only, both or neither, and that a regular figure with n sides has n lines and n angles of symmetry.

content.text:
$1$. $(a)$: Only an equilateral triangle has $2$ or more lines.
$2$. $(b)$: An isosceles triangle folds one way only and fits only after $360^\circ$.
$3$. $(c)$: A slanted parallelogram fits after a half turn but cannot be folded. $(d)$: An isosceles trapezium folds down the middle but a half turn does not fit.
Answer: $(a)$: Equilateral triangle: $3$ lines, $3$ angles, namely $120^\circ$, $240^\circ$, $360^\circ$. $(b)$: Isosceles triangle (not equilateral): $1$ line, no rotational symmetry. $(c)$: Parallelogram that is not a rectangle or rhombus: no line, angles $180^\circ$ and $360^\circ$. $(d)$: Isosceles trapezium: $1$ line, no rotational symmetry.

media.title: Tile Designer
media.context: Class 6 NCERT Ganita Prakash ch 9 'Symmetry' (Both Together, Tiles and a Game). Place and turn tiles to make symmetrical designs. Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description:
The student gets a 4 by 4 board and a tray of 16 square tiles. Each tile is cut along one diagonal into a blue triangle and a yellow triangle, so it can be turned into four different looks. Above the board are a Check Lines button, a Check Turns button and a counter for the lines and angles of symmetry found.

The student predicts the number of lines, then places tiles in the cells and turns each one a quarter turn at a time. A tile and its mirror partner across a vertical line must slope the opposite way, with the blue and yellow triangles mirrored too. Check Lines tests the vertical line, the horizontal line and both diagonals, and draws each line of symmetry it finds as a dashed line. If a line is missing, the tile that has no partner is highlighted. If the design has an extra line, such as a diagonal, the line is drawn on the design so the student sees there are too many. Check Turns tests the turns and lists the angles found. For the half turn, each tile must match the tile opposite it after a turn of 180 degrees, as the tile in the top left corner must match the one in the bottom right.

The six tasks are: make a design with exactly 1 line of symmetry; exactly 2 lines; 4 lines; a half turn but no line; complete a given quarter of the board into a design with exactly 2 lines and no diagonal line; and make a design with no line and no turn, so that only 360 degrees works. A solved card shows the lines and the turns found.

Hints come in order. First: what must each tile match for a line to work? Then: fill one part, then copy it across the line you want. Then: check for extra lines, especially along the diagonals. Last, the tile with no partner is highlighted: fix it and check again. Through doing, the student learns that a line of symmetry needs every tile to match its mirror partner, that extra lines must be checked before counting, and that a design can be symmetric by a turn even when it has no line.

concepts.concept_name: Completing a tile design with two lines

content.text:
Draw a 6 by 6 grid. Two players take turns covering two adjacent squares by drawing a line. The line can be placed either way: horizontally or vertically. The lines cannot overlap. The game goes on till a player is not able to place any more lines. The player who is not able to place a line loses.
With what strategy can one play to win this game?

content.publication_text:
Draw a 6 by 6 grid. Two players take turns covering two adjacent squares by drawing a line. The line can be placed either way: horizontally or vertically. The lines cannot overlap. The game goes on till a player is not able to place any more lines. The player who is not able to place a line loses.
With what strategy can one play to win this game?

content.text:
1. Predict first: two players cover two adjacent squares with a line in turn, and the player who cannot place a line loses. Who do you think wins?
2. The centre of the 6 by 6 grid is a corner point where 4 squares meet, so no line covers it.
3. After each move of the first player, the second player places a line on its 180° rotation about the centre. That place is free, so the second player always has a reply.
4. The first player runs out of moves first, so the second player wins.

content.text:
$1$. Reflect the filled top-left quarter across the vertical red line into the top-right quarter.
$2$. Reflect the top half across the horizontal red line into the bottom half.
$3$. Check that no other fold line works.
Answer: Fill the other three quarters as mirror images of the filled quarter in the red lines (reflect across the vertical line, then across the horizontal line). The result has exactly $2$ lines of symmetry, the two red lines.

content.text:
$1$. Lay $16$ tiles in a $4$ by $4$ square.
$2$. For $1$ line, make the left half a mirror image of the right half only.
$3$. For $2$ lines, make it a mirror image both left to right and top to bottom, but not along the diagonals.
Answer: Open ended. A correct $4$ by $4$ arrangement has exactly one fold line (for example a vertical line) in the first case, and exactly two fold lines (for example vertical and horizontal) in the second.

concepts.concept_name: Playing with Tiles and a Symmetry Game: Q4

content.text:
$1$. The centre of the $6$ by $6$ grid is a corner point where $4$ squares meet, so no line can cover it.
$2$. Every first-player move has a rotated copy that is free and does not overlap it.
$3$. So the second player always has a reply and the first player runs out of moves first.
Answer: The second player wins: after each move of the first player, place a line that is the $180^\circ$ rotation about the centre of the grid of that move.

topics.summary: Lines of symmetry and reflection, angles of symmetry and rotation, the circle, and how the two ideas relate.

content.text:
When a figure is made up of parts that repeat in a definite pattern, we say that the figure has symmetry. We say that such a figure is symmetrical.
A line that cuts a plane figure into two parts that exactly overlap when folded along that line is called a line of symmetry or axis of symmetry of the figure.
A figure may have multiple lines of symmetry.
Sometimes a figure looks exactly the same when it is rotated by an angle about a fixed point. Such an angle is called an angle of symmetry of the figure. A figure that has an angle of symmetry strictly between 0 and 360 degrees is said to have rotational symmetry. The point of the figure about which the rotation occurs is called the centre of rotation.
A figure may have multiple angles of symmetry.
Some figures may have a line of symmetry but no angle of symmetry, while others may have angles of symmetry but no lines of symmetry. Some figures may have both lines of symmetry as well as angles of symmetry.

objectives.objective_text: Students fold a figure along a dotted line, decide whether the two halves overlap exactly, and call such halves mirror halves.
Students define a line of symmetry as a line that cuts a figure into two parts that overlap exactly when folded, and name the vertical line of symmetry of a building.
Students fold a figure on the tool along a chosen line, check whether the halves overlap, and list the lines of symmetry the figure has, including none.
Students fold a square vertically, horizontally and along both diagonals, and conclude that a square has exactly 4 lines of symmetry.
Students list all the lines of symmetry of a design by trying every direction, and say when a design has no line at all.
Students test the diagonal of a rectangle that is not a square by folding, and explain why the two triangles do not overlap.
Students count the lines of symmetry of squares, stars, regular shapes and kolam patterns, and draw triangles and curved figures with a given number of lines.
Students state where corners A, B, C and D of a square go when it is reflected in the vertical line of symmetry.
Students find where the corners of a square go for a reflection in a diagonal and in the horizontal line, and say which corners stay fixed.
Students reflect each point of a half-figure in a given mirror line and complete the figure so that the line, or both lines, are lines of symmetry.
Students make an ink blot on one half of a folded sheet and name the crease as the line of symmetry of the pattern.
Students predict the opened shape after a cut on a folded sheet, and identify the fold as the line of symmetry of the opened shape.
Students fold a strip several times, cut a pattern, and find the lines of symmetry of the repeating design.
Students punch or cut a folded sheet on the tool, unfold it, and find the fold lines that match a given pattern of holes or a given opened shape.
Students explain that a windmill with 4 equal blades looks the same after a 90° turn about its centre, and define the centre of rotation and an angle of symmetry.
Students list the angles of symmetry of a square and mark its centre of rotation at the crossing of the diagonals.
Students show by turning that a strip with one short side does not match itself after 180°, so its only angle of symmetry is 360°.
Students turn a figure about its marked centre on the tool, note each turn at which it matches itself, and list the angles of symmetry.
Students list the 4 angles of symmetry of a figure with 4 equal arms 90° apart, and check by turning a cut-out copy.
Students change a 4-arm figure to have only 2 angles of symmetry, and show that 3 arms with unequal angles give only 360°.
Students show that three arms give 3 angles of symmetry only when each angle between arms is 360 ÷ 3 = 120°, and list the angles 120°, 240° and 360°.
Students set the number of arms and the angles between them on the tool, turn the figure, and give its angles of symmetry and its order.
Students find the smallest angle of symmetry of figures with 5, 6 and 7 equal arms as 360 ÷ n, and write it as a mixed fraction when it is not whole.
Students explain that the angles of symmetry of a figure are the multiples of its smallest angle and that 360° is always one of them.
Students pick the number of equal turns on the tool, read the smallest angle 360 ÷ n and the ladder of its multiples, and decide whether a given smallest angle is possible.
Students explain that a circle looks the same after a turn of any angle, so it has no smallest angle of symmetry.
Students show that every diameter of a circle is a line of symmetry, so the circle has endless lines of symmetry.
Students name everyday objects that look the same after a turn, such as wheels and fan blades, and give how many turns each has.
Students count the lines of symmetry and the angles of symmetry of a wheel with equal spokes such as the Ashoka Chakra.
Students give an example of a figure with a line of symmetry but no rotational symmetry, and one with rotational symmetry but no line, and explain why one does not imply the other.
Students count the lines and the angles of symmetry of a square and an equilateral triangle, and see that a regular figure with n sides has n of each.
Students sort figures on the tool by lines of symmetry and angles of symmetry, and sketch figures that have a stated mix of the two.
Students complete a tile figure by reflecting the filled quarter so that it has exactly 2 lines of symmetry.
Students explain why the second player always wins the 6 by 6 line-placing game by answering each move with its 180° rotation about the centre of the grid.
Students lay colour tiles on a 4 by 4 grid on the tool, and make designs with exactly 1 line, exactly 2 lines, or a turn of symmetry.
Students restate the meaning of a line of symmetry, an angle of symmetry and the centre of rotation, and say which figures have lines, turns, both or neither.

video_coverage.book_item: Book item: A blue triangle has a dotted line down its middle. If you fold the triangle along the dotted line, does one half cover the other half completely? Now look at four puzzle pieces joined together with a dotted line through the middle. Are the two sides mirror halves?

Book item: Look at the pictures of the Taj Mahal and the Gopuram (a temple tower). What are the symmetries that you see in these beautiful structures? Why is the picture of the clouds not symmetrical?
Book item: Do you see any line of symmetry in the pictures at the start of the chapter (flower, butterfly, rangoli, pinwheel)? What about the picture of the cloud?

Book item: For each of the following figures, identify the line(s) of symmetry if it exists. The five figures, in order, are: (1) an irregular pentagon-like shape with a notch (arrow-head like), (2) a kite, (3) a quadrilateral with two right angles and a slanted top, (4) an L-shape, (5) a scalene triangle. 1) Arrow-head like pentagon with a notch 2) Kite 3) Quadrilateral with slanted top and two right angles 4) L-shape 5) Scalene triangle
Book item: Does a square have only one line of symmetry? Take a square piece of paper and, by folding, find all its lines of symmetry.
Book item: Is there any other way to fold the square so that the two halves overlap? How many lines of symmetry does the square shape have?

Book item: Find all the lines of symmetry of each of three figures: (1) a red outline ring with spiky triangular points around it (like a Koch snowflake), (2) a yellow flower of six curved petals meeting at a red-marked centre, (3) a green looped design with four round loops at the corners and a small square in the centre.

Book item: We saw that the diagonal of a square is also a line of symmetry. Take a rectangle that is not a square. Is its diagonal a line of symmetry? First see the rectangle and answer, then take a rectangular piece of paper and check by folding along its diagonal whether the two parts overlap.

Book item: How many lines of symmetry do these shapes have? (a) a square drawn tilted like a diamond, and an eight-pointed star shape; (b) a triangle with equal sides and equal angles; (c) a hexagon with equal sides and equal angles. a) square drawn like a diamond; eight-pointed star b) triangle with equal sides and equal angles c) hexagon with equal sides and equal angles

Book item: Trace each figure and draw the lines of symmetry, if any. There are eight figures: four rhombus-pattern figures (1: one rhombus sitting on top of two rhombi that touch each other; 2: three rhombi in a row joined at their left-right corners; 3: a large diamond made of four small rhombi; 4: four rhombi in two columns of two, overlapping, standing in an X-like arrangement) and four figures on squared grids (5: a square inside a bigger square with the inner square divided into four; 6: an octagon-like shape with long vertical sides; 7: a five-sided shape like a kite with a flat right side; 8: a four-pointed star). 1) rhombus pattern 1 (one rhombus above two) 2) three rhombi in a row 3) large diamond of four rhombi 4) four overlapping rhombi, two columns 5) square inside a square on grid 6) octagon-like shape on grid 7) five-sided shape on grid 8) four-pointed star on grid

Book item: Find the lines of symmetry for the kolam below. The kolam is a large six-sided (hexagonal) pattern made of dots and star shapes made of rhombi, with the same design repeating around the centre.

Book item: Draw the following. (a) A triangle with exactly one line of symmetry. (b) A triangle with exactly three lines of symmetry. (c) A triangle with no line of symmetry. Is it possible to draw a triangle with exactly two lines of symmetry? a) triangle with exactly one line of symmetry b) triangle with exactly three lines of symmetry c) triangle with no line of symmetry d) Is it possible to draw a triangle with exactly two lines of symmetry?

Book item: Draw the following. In each case, the figure should contain at least one curved boundary. (a) A figure with exactly one line of symmetry. (b) A figure with exactly two lines of symmetry. (c) A figure with exactly four lines of symmetry. a) exactly one line of symmetry, with a curved boundary b) exactly two lines of symmetry, with a curved boundary c) exactly four lines of symmetry, with a curved boundary
Book item: A square has corners labelled A (top left), B (top right), C (bottom right), D (bottom left). When the square is reflected along the vertical line of symmetry, where do A, B, C and D go?

Book item: For the same square ABCD (A top left, B top right, C bottom right, D bottom left): what if we reflect along the diagonal from A to C? Where do points A, B, C and D go? What if we reflect along the horizontal line of symmetry?

Book item: Copy the following on squared paper. Complete them so that the blue line is a line of symmetry. Problem (a) has been done for you. (b) A stepped red shape above a horizontal blue line, with a slanted edge ending at the right end of the line. (c) A staircase-shaped red outline next to a slanted (diagonal) blue line. (d) A small red shape touching a vertical blue line on a narrow grid. (e) A red five-sided outline hanging below a horizontal blue line. (f) A red outline with corner cuts next to a diagonal blue line. Hint: for (c) and (f), see if rotating the book helps! b) red stepped shape above a horizontal blue line c) staircase outline beside a diagonal blue line d) small shape on a vertical line e) five-sided red outline hanging below a horizontal line f) red outline with corner cuts beside a diagonal line

Book item: Copy the following drawing on squared paper. Complete each one of them so that the resulting figure has the two blue lines as lines of symmetry. (a) two diagonal blue lines crossing, with a red horizontal segment near the bottom; (b) two diagonal blue lines crossing, with a red broken vertical segment with a point on the left; (c) a vertical and a horizontal blue line, with a stepped red outline in the upper left; (d) a vertical and a horizontal blue line, with a red corner outline in the lower left; (e) a vertical and a horizontal blue line, with a red zigzag in the upper right; (f) a vertical and a horizontal blue line, with a red outline in the lower left. a) diagonals, red bottom segment b) diagonals, red left zigzag c) vertical and horizontal, stepped upper-left outline d) vertical and horizontal, lower-left corner outline e) vertical and horizontal, upper-right zigzag f) vertical and horizontal, lower-left outline
Book item: Copy the following on a dot grid. For each figure draw two more lines to make a shape that has a line of symmetry. The six dot-grid figures each show a few connected line segments.

Book item: Take a piece of paper and fold it in half. Open it and spill a few drops of ink (or paint) on one half. Press the halves together and open the paper again. What do you see? Is the resulting figure symmetric? If yes, where is the line of symmetry? Is there any other line along which it can be folded to produce two identical parts? Try making more such patterns.

Book item: In two pictures, a sheet of paper is folded and a cut is made along the dotted line shown (the dotted line forms a notch shape starting at the fold). Draw a sketch of how the paper will look when unfolded. Do you see a line of symmetry in this figure? What is it?

Book item: Make different symmetric shapes by folding and cutting. Use thin rectangular coloured paper, fold it several times and cut out intricate patterns, like the blue star-shaped cut-outs shown. Identify the lines of symmetry in the repeating design.

Book item: In each of the following figures, a hole was punched in a folded square sheet of paper and then the paper was unfolded. Identify the line along which the paper was folded. The four unfolded sheets show: (a) two holes in the left and right sides at the same height; (b) two holes close together near the top right corner; (c) two holes on the right edge, one above the other; (d) four holes, one near each corner. Figure (d) was created by punching a single hole. How was the paper folded? a) two holes, one on the left and one on the right at the same height b) two holes close together near the top right corner c) two holes on the right edge, one above the other d) four holes near the four corners (made with a single hole)

Book item: Given the line(s) of symmetry, find the other hole(s). Five shapes each show one hole and a dashed line of symmetry: (a) a square with a diagonal from top left to bottom right and a hole near the top left; (b) a square with a horizontal middle line and a hole in the lower right; (c) an equilateral triangle with a vertical line through the apex and a hole just left of the line near the middle; (d) a circle with a slanted diameter and a hole above the line near the right; (e) a circle with a diagonal line from top left to bottom right and a hole near the top left, close to the line. a) square, diagonal line, hole near top left b) square, horizontal middle line, hole lower right c) triangle, vertical line, hole left of the line d) circle, slanted diameter, hole above the line e) circle, diagonal line, hole near top left

Book item: Here are some questions on paper cutting. Consider a vertical fold. We represent it by a picture of a sheet folded in half vertically with an arrow. Similarly, a horizontal fold is represented by a sheet folded in half horizontally with an arrow.

Book item: After each of the following cuts, predict the shape of the hole when the paper is opened. After you have made your prediction, make the cutouts and verify your answer. (a) A green sheet is folded once; a wavy cut is made from the edge, along a dotted line, with a narrow pinched middle. (b) A green sheet is folded once; a cut shaped like a notched banner (with an arrow-head notch) is made. (c) A purple sheet is folded vertically and then horizontally (4 layers) and notches are cut at the corner and edge. (d) A yellow sheet is folded vertically once and rectangular notches are cut along the open edge. a) green sheet folded once, wavy cut near the open edge b) green sheet folded once, banner-shaped cut with an arrow-head notch c) purple sheet folded twice (vertical then horizontal), notches cut d) yellow sheet folded vertically, notches cut along the open edge

Book item: Suppose you have to get each of these shapes with some folds and a single straight cut. How will you do it? (a) The hole in the centre is a square (sides parallel to the sides of the sheet). (b) The hole in the centre is a square (tilted so that its corners point up, down, left and right). Note: for the above two questions, check if the 4-sided figures in the centre satisfy both the properties of a square. a) square hole in the centre with sides parallel to the paper b) tilted square hole in the centre

Book item: Look at the rangoli picture (a round flower-like design with a ring in the centre and four red petals around it). Can you see what repeats in it? What happens to the red petals when the rangoli is rotated by 90° around the centre?

Book item: A paper windmill with 4 equal blades looks the same when turned by 90° about the red point at its centre. Will the windmill look exactly the same when rotated through an angle of less than 90°?
Book item: The windmill has exactly 4 angles of symmetry: 90°, 180°, 270° and 360°. Do you know of any other shape that has exactly four angles of symmetry?
Book item: How many angles of symmetry does a square have? How much rotation does it require to get the initial square?
Book item: A square gets back onto itself after a 90° rotation. Do you know where to mark the centre of rotation?
Book item: What are the other angles of symmetry of a square (besides 90°)?

Book item: Find the angles of symmetry of the following strip. The strip is a trapezium shape (the top side is shorter than the bottom side, the two slanting sides are equal) with a dot marking its centre.
Book item: After the strip is rotated by 180° about its centre, does it overlap with the original strip? Why?

Book item: Find the angles of symmetry for the given figures about the point marked with a dot. (a) A plus shape made of a vertical rectangle and a horizontal rectangle of the same length crossing at their middles, dot at the centre. (b) A vertical line with a dot at its middle, and a small square on the right of the top end and another small square on the right of the bottom end. (c) A horizontal segment joining the middles of two long vertical lines (a sideways H), dot at the middle of the horizontal segment. a) Plus shape of two equal rectangles. b) Vertical line with a small square on the right of each end. c) Horizontal bar joining two vertical lines.

Book item: Which of the following figures have more than one angle of symmetry? The seven figures are: a circle with a cross dividing it into 4 equal parts; a downward-pointing triangle with a dot inside; a circle divided into 3 equal parts by three spokes; a four-bladed pinwheel with a red cross; an X made of two crossing lines; a five-pointed star with a dot at its centre; a shape like the letter B made of a vertical line with two half circles on its right.
Book item: A picture has 4 radial arms (a plus-shaped figure with 4 equal arms), and the angle between adjacent central dotted lines is 90°. How many angles of symmetry does it have? What are they?
Book item: Can you change the angles between the radial arms so that the figure still has 4 angles of symmetry? Try drawing it.

Book item: To check if a figure with radial arms has 4 angles of symmetry, draw it on two pieces of paper. Cut out the radial arms from one paper, keep the figure on the other paper fixed, and rotate the cutout to check for rotational symmetry.
Book item: How will you modify the plus-shaped figure with 4 radial arms so that it has only two angles of symmetry?
Book item: Can we get a figure having exactly 3 angles of symmetry? Can you use radial arms for this?
Book item: A figure has 3 radial arms but the angles between the arms are not equal. How many angles of symmetry does it have and what are they?
Book item: Can anything in the three-arm figure be changed to make it have 3 angles of symmetry? Can it be done by changing the angles between the dotted lines?

Book item: If a figure with three radial arms has rotational symmetry, a rotated copy must overlap the original. What can you tell about the angles ∠A, ∠B and ∠C between the arms? What must this angle be?
Book item: A 3-arm figure has 120° between adjacent arms. How many angles of rotation does it have and what are they?

Book item: Give the order of rotational symmetry for each figure: (a) a slanted line with a small flag at its top left end and another small flag at its bottom right end, dot at its middle; (b) an X made of two crossing lines with an angle marked at the top; (c) a six-pointed star with a dot at the centre; (d) three bent arms with fists arranged around a centre; (e) a plus shape made of two rectangles with a dot at the centre; (f) a regular pentagon with a dot at the centre. a) Slanted line with flags at its two ends b) X of two crossing lines c) Six-pointed star d) Three bent arms with fists e) Plus shape f) Regular pentagon

Book item: Look at the pinwheel picture (a blue figure made of many triangles arranged around a hexagon). Which pattern is repeating? Hint: look at the hexagon first. What figure repeats along each side of the hexagon, what is its shape, and how do these shapes move as you go along the boundary of the hexagon?

Book item: Can you draw a figure with radial arms that has a) exactly 5 angles of symmetry, b) 6 angles of symmetry? Also find the angles of symmetry in each case. Hint: Use 5 radial arms for the first case. What should the angle between two adjacent radial arms be? a) Figure with radial arms having exactly 5 angles of symmetry; list the angles. b) Figure with radial arms having 6 angles of symmetry; list the angles.

Book item: Consider a figure with radial arms having exactly 7 angles of symmetry. What will be its smallest angle of symmetry? Is the number of degrees a whole number in this case? If not, express it as a mixed fraction.

Book item: Angles of symmetry when there are exactly 2 of them: 180°, 360°. Exactly 3 of them: 120°, 240°, 360°. Exactly 4 of them: 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°. In each case, the angles are the multiples of the smallest angle. Will this always happen? What do you think?

Book item: True or False: (1) Every figure will have 360 degrees as an angle of symmetry. (2) If the smallest angle of symmetry of a figure is a natural number in degrees, then it is a factor of 360. 1) Every figure will have 360 degrees as an angle of symmetry. 2) If the smallest angle of symmetry of a figure is a natural number in degrees, then it is a factor of 360.

Book item: Colour the sectors of the circle below so that the figure has i) 3 angles of symmetry, ii) 4 angles of symmetry, iii) what are the possible numbers of angles of symmetry you can obtain by colouring the sectors in different ways? The circle is divided into 12 equal sectors. i) 3 angles of symmetry ii) 4 angles of symmetry iii) Possible numbers of angles of symmetry
Book item: In a figure, 60° is the smallest angle of symmetry. What are the other angles of symmetry of this figure?
Book item: In a figure, 60° is an angle of symmetry. The figure has two angles of symmetry less than 60°. What is its smallest angle of symmetry?
Book item: Can we have a figure with rotational symmetry whose smallest angle of symmetry is: a. 45°? b. 17°? a) Smallest angle of symmetry 45° b) Smallest angle of symmetry 17°
Book item: Is there a smallest angle of symmetry for all figures?
Book item: Take a point on the rim of a circle and join it to the centre. Extend the segment to a diameter. Is that diameter a line of reflection symmetry?
Book item: Like wheels, we can find other objects around us having rotational symmetry. Find them. (Shown: a three-bladed fan, a five-petal flower, a wheel with many spokes.)
Book item: How many lines of symmetry and angles of symmetry does Ashoka Chakra have? (The Ashoka Chakra is a wheel with 24 equal spokes.)
Book item: Draw two figures other than a circle and a square that have both reflection symmetry and rotational symmetry.

Book item: Draw, wherever possible, a rough sketch of: a. A triangle with at least two lines of symmetry and at least two angles of symmetry. b. A triangle with only one line of symmetry but not having rotational symmetry. c. A quadrilateral with rotational symmetry but no reflection symmetry. d. A quadrilateral with reflection symmetry but not having rotational symmetry. a) Triangle with at least two lines and two angles of symmetry b) Triangle with only one line of symmetry, no rotational symmetry c) Quadrilateral with rotational symmetry but no reflection symmetry d) Quadrilateral with reflection symmetry, no rotational symmetry

Book item: This is a picture of the new Parliament Building in Delhi; its outer boundary is a triangle-like shape with its three corners cut off (3 long sides alternating with 3 short sides). a. Does the outer boundary of the picture have reflection symmetry? If so, draw the lines of symmetries. How many are they? b. Does it have rotational symmetry around its centre? If so, find the angles of rotational symmetry. a) Reflection symmetry? Number of lines b) Rotational symmetry? Angles

Book item: How many lines of symmetry do the shapes in the first shape sequence in Chapter 1, Table 3, the Regular Polygons, have? What number sequence do you get? (The shapes are the regular triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon, heptagon, octagon, nonagon and decagon.)

Book item: How many angles of symmetry do the shapes in the first shape sequence in Chapter 1, Table 3, the Regular Polygons, have? What number sequence do you get? (Regular triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon, heptagon, octagon, nonagon, decagon.)

Book item: How many lines of symmetry do the shapes in the last shape sequence in Chapter 1, Table 3, the Koch Snowflake sequence, have? How many angles of symmetry? lines) Lines of symmetry for the 5 shapes angles) Angles of symmetry for the 5 shapes

Book item: Use the colour tiles given at the end of the book to complete the following figure so that it has exactly 2 lines of symmetry. (An 8 by 8 grid of square tiles, each divided by a diagonal into a blue and a yellow triangle. The top left 4 by 4 quarter is already filled. A red vertical line and a red horizontal line pass through the middle of the grid.)

Book item: Draw a 6 by 6 grid. Two players take turns covering two adjacent squares by drawing a line. The line can be placed either way: horizontally or vertically. The lines cannot overlap. The game goes on till a player is not able to place any more lines. The player who is not able to place a line loses. With what strategy can one play to win this game?
Book item: Use 16 such colour tiles to make figures that have exactly: 1 line of symmetry; 2 lines of symmetry. 1) Figure with exactly 1 line of symmetry 2) Figure with exactly 2 lines of symmetry
Book item: Use these colour tiles in making creative symmetric designs.

restructure.note: Order and home of questions only. Teaching text, objectives, tools and rendered videos are carried over; question and solution images are placeholders until the solutions are authored.
restructure.layout: concept topic, then its Questions topic (one concept per book question: solved example, exercise, answerable prompt), then the next concept topic

chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's order. Folding paper finds lines of symmetry, turning cut-outs finds angles of symmetry, and each idea is tested on rangoli, kolam, wheels and tiles from everyday life.

points.text: Every new idea starts from a paper fold or a paper turn, so a line of symmetry and an angle of symmetry are first seen, then named.
points.title: Fold it, turn it, then say it

points.text: Each idea gets its own topic: worked videos for the book's questions, a tool only where handling the figure is the idea, then the book's Figure it Out questions in a practice topic, each with its own video.
points.title: Concept, then practice, topic by topic

points.text: A figure may have lines, turns, both or neither, and the plan keeps the two ideas apart until the chapter brings them together.
points.title: Lines and turns are different

points.text: The common wrong ideas, such as 'the diagonal of a rectangle is a line of symmetry', are raised by Keeko and fixed with a fold or a cut-out, never just a rule.
points.title: Keeko's doubts

chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
